title.value: Mortality trends and length of stays among hospitalized patients with COVID-19 in Ontario and Québec (Canada): a population-based cohort study of the first three epidemic waves
title.justification: The title directly reflects the content of the paper, focusing on mortality trends and hospital stay lengths for COVID-19 patients during the first three COVID-19 waves in Ontario and Québec, Canada.
title.quote: Mortality trends and length of stays among hospitalized patients with COVID-19 in Ontario and Québec (Canada): a population-based cohort study of the first three epidemic waves

extractions.description: This study analyzes hospital data from Ontario and Québec, focusing on trends in mortality and length of stays of COVID-19 patients during the first three waves of the pandemic. It aims to provide insights into mortality risks and ICU stay durations, particularly under varying levels of hospital load. The paper discusses factors influencing mortality trends, including vaccination, age, and hospital-acquired infections.

sustainable_development_is_central.justification: The paper primarily discusses healthcare outcomes related to COVID-19, such as mortality trends and hospital stay lengths in Canada, rather than focusing on broader Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development themes.
sustainable_development_is_central.quote: Background: Epidemics of COVID-19 strained hospital resources. We describe temporal trends in mortality risk and length of stays in hospital and intensive care units (ICUs) among patients with COVID-19 hospitalized through the first three epidemic waves in Canada.

primary_category.justification: The study is centered around public health and healthcare resource management during the COVID-19 pandemic, which does not align directly with Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development categories.
primary_category.quote: In-hospital mortality risks and length of ICU stays declined over time despite changing patient demographics. Continuous population-based monitoring of patient outcomes in an evolving epidemic is necessary for health system preparedness and response.

secondary_categories.justification: There are no additional themes in the paper that align with the listed Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development categories.
secondary_categories.quote: Our study should be interpreted considering certain limitations. First, we were unable to control for sex, ethnicity, and comorbidities—factors that could be associated with COVID-19 mortality.

primary_sub_category.justification: The content of the paper does not fall under any specific sub-category related to Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development.
primary_sub_category.quote: Strengths of this study includes its representativeness: all hospitalizations in these two provinces are included.

secondary_sub_categories.justification: There are no additional sub-themes in the paper that align with Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development sub-categories.
secondary_sub_categories.quote: First, we were unable to control for sex, ethnicity, and comorbidities—factors that could be associated with COVID-19 mortality.

new_primary_category.justification: The study focuses on public health indicators, such as mortality trends and ICU stay length, in the context of COVID-19, indicating a need for categorizing under Public Health and Epidemiology.
new_primary_category.quote: Understanding the drivers of in-hospital COVID-19 mortality is important to improve the accuracy of those projections.

new_primary_sub_category.justification: Given the paper's focus on hospital resources, patient load, and outcomes during COVID-19, it would best fit a sub-category related to healthcare resource management.
new_primary_sub_category.quote: Projections of future demands for hospital beds have helped decision-makers to manage and allocate limited healthcare resources.
